title: Head-to-head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes
abstract: We report a preregistered, paired comparison (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) of two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). Generation used gpt‑5‑mini and end‑to‑end correctness used a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that checks syntax, workflow constraints, and emulator reachability/isolation. Critically, the preregistration specified shared_initial_candidate generation semantics so both arms received the same LLM candidate per task. The confirmatory paired design executed 120 task pairs (240 episodes planned) with one shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). All completed episodes passed the deterministic validator in both arms (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A−B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We therefore report operational parity under the specific preregistered constraints and document—using archived artifacts—(1) that only a single shared LLM generation stage was executed per pair, (2) no repairs were applied (repair_applied=false in validator traces), and (3) the run therefore measured validator acceptance of identical candidates rather than independent-generation robustness. We discuss implications, threats to validity, representative artifacts, and minimal experimental changes required to discriminate architectures in future studies.

sections.introduction: The emergence of foundation models and agentic LLM pipelines presents opportunities and risks for automating NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change sequencing, and limited self‑healing. Operational correctness—ensuring network reachability, policy isolation, and avoiding unsafe transients during changes—is nonnegotiable. Prior literature spans translator→verifier toolchains that rely on formal models and solvers, and agentic systems that iteratively generate, validate, and repair proposals. However, systematic, preregistered, paired head‑to‑head comparisons using deterministic validators are rare. We ask: For intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulated topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness: (A) translation‑first (constrained DSL→verifier→solver) or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair using a hosted LLM plus deterministic validators and bounded rollback? Contributions. (i) A machine‑readable preregistered paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) executed on 120 paired tasks with explicit shared_initial_candidate semantics; (ii) a complete, archived execution and analysis bundle (execution/*, analysis/*) that shows which processing stages ran and the per‑task validator traces; (iii) a confirmatory result showing parity under these constraints and an explicit artefact‑grounded explanation of why the run did not exercise independent generation or repair.
sections.related_work: Network verification has long used formal translation and model checking to obtain provable properties when device models exist. Recent NetOps literature explores LLMs for intent translation and agentic management, emphasizing the role of validators, checkers, and rollback contracts in achieving operational reliability. Work such as intent‑translation systems and verification frameworks motivates direct comparison of architectural choices, but prior evaluations rarely couple preregistration, deterministic validators, and paired designs that isolate downstream behavior. Our study positions itself within this body by focusing on operational correctness and by making the shared generation and validation semantics explicit and artifact‑traceable.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The study was fully preregistered (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) and frozen prior to observing outcomes. Primary estimand: paired difference in binary end‑to‑end operational correctness (A − B). Confirmatory sample: n=120 paired tasks balanced across vendor×topology clusters. Generation model: gpt‑5‑mini (declared_model_version). Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). Important preregistered design choice—shared_initial_candidate: the execution contract specified that both pipelines receive the identical LLM candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate generation semantics). This choice was implemented and recorded in provider traces and per‑task scoring artifacts (see representative scoring artifact execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json). Execution and stages. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter executed the preregistered pipeline. Deterministic reconciliation and provider_call_audit show a single shared generation stage per pair (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 120) and model_calls_used = 120 (analysis/artifacts: analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; execution/model_configuration.json). Per‑task validator traces (execution/scoring/*.json) record validator decisions and whether repairs were applied. Scoring and analysis. End‑to‑end correctness was a binary outcome: final configuration accepted by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (syntax, per‑interface dependency rules, required sequence checks, and emulator reachability/isolation). Primary analysis used paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and McNemar exact two‑sided test executed by paired_binary_analysis_v1 (archived analysis artifacts and logs). Planned secondary estimands (repair coverage, mean repair iterations) were recorded but require repair events to be informative.

Deterministic reconciliation. Provider_call_audit and reconciliation artifacts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirm that only a single shared generation stage executed per pair (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=120) and that no cross‑condition cache reuse occurred.
sections.discussion: What the data show. Under the exact preregistered conditions—most notably shared_initial_candidate semantics, single hosted LLM generation per pair, and deterministic validator acceptance—both architectures produced validator‑satisfying outputs for every included task. The run therefore demonstrates parity in validator acceptance when the same candidate is supplied to both pipelines and when the validator is sufficiently constraining. What the data do not show. Because the experiment intentionally removed independent generation variance and because no repairs were triggered, the run does not test (a) whether one architecture produces better independent candidates under identical budget constraints, (b) whether agentic repair would rescue initially failing proposals more often than a translation→solver route, or (c) how architectures behave under nondeterministic or weaker validators. Artifact‑backed reasons. (1) Shared generation accounting: model_calls_used = 120 (execution manifest) and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation":120} (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) show only the shared generation stage ran; this explains why model call accounting differs from the episode count (240 planned episodes vs 120 model calls). (2) No repairs applied: every per‑task scoring JSON includes validator_trace.repair_applied = false (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json), demonstrating that repair loops did not run because initial candidates satisfied validator constraints. Ceiling effect and inferential limits. The primary confirmatory test is uninformative for superiority due to a ceiling effect (all pairs succeeded in both arms; n_10 = n_01 = 0). We therefore reframe the confirmatory conclusion: this experiment shows validator‑acceptance parity under a shared‑candidate, deterministic‑validator regime, not general architectural equivalence. Practical operational implication. The result highlights the decisive role of verifier/validator machinery and change contracts: when a high‑fidelity deterministic validator exists and an acceptable candidate is available, both architectures can reach the same validator‑defined operational correctness. Recommendations for discriminating designs. To compare architectures' intrinsic generation and repair robustness, minimally (i) run independent generation per arm (remove shared_initial_candidate), (ii) allow separate per‑arm model budgets and repair budgets, (iii) exercise multiple LLMs and validator strictness levels, and (iv) evaluate on higher‑fidelity device images or hardware; these changes are precisely those preregistered as follow‑ups in the study plan.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired comparison of a translation‑first pipeline and an agentic generate→validate→repair pipeline over 120 intent task pairs using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic NetOps validator. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and deterministic validation, both pipelines produced validator‑satisfying configurations for all tasks (100% success each), yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). Artifact traces show only a single shared LLM generation per pair and no repair activity; therefore, the run measured validator acceptance of identical candidates rather than independent architectural robustness. We provide artifact‑grounded evidence for each factual claim and recommend targeted preregistered experiments (independent generation, multi‑model, varied validator strictness, higher‑fidelity execution) that are necessary to discriminate architectures under operational realism.

The run deliberately used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (preregistered); both pipeline arms received the same initial LLM candidate per task, as recorded in the per‑task provider traces and scoring artifacts (representative examples: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json). limitations: Shared_initial_candidate generation semantics were preregistered and used; this intentionally removes variance from the generation stage and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.
Task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
Single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied=false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

Deterministic validator decisions can mask subtle behavioral differences (e.g., human‑operator readability, explanation quality) that matter in operational practice but were outside the formal end‑to‑end correctness metric used here.
